1.0 EXPLORATION AND EVALUATION SUMMARY

Well 25/7-3 was a discretionary exploration well located approximately 112 km WNW of Stavanger. The primary objective of the well was to prove up commercial reserves for the 25/7-3 structure (Elli South) by testing the hydrocarbon potential of the Paleocene Upper Heimdal Formation.

Block 25/7 is situated in the South Viking Graben on the western side of the Utsira High, a basement high that tilts slightly towards the east. The South Viking Graben has an asymmetrical profile bounded in the west by the Brae/Crawford Fault Zone and the Utsira High to the east. The Elli Field is located on a basement terrace stepping up to the Utsira High from the Graben area.

Operations began when the semisubmersible drilling rig Deepsea Bergen was picked up in Haugesund on 26 July 1995. Well 25/7-3 was spudded on 27 July.

Two cores were cut in the Heimdal Formation, both with full recovery. The first core was cut 2099-2110.6m RKB, and the second at 2111-2130.2 m RKB. Shows were described in the cores down to a depth of 2117m RKB.

A total of 20 FMT pressure tests were taken, with 19 successfully recorded. An oil sample was taken at the depth of 2112 m RKB. The fluid was described as medium to dark brown with moderate viscosity and dull to intermediate white to pale yellow direct fluorescence.

The well was drilled vertical to a total depth of 2540m RKB into the Upper Cretaceous Tor Formation. The well was permanently plugged and abandoned and the rig was released at the 25/7-3 location on 28 August 1995 at 2230 hrs.

One drill stem test was performed in the Heimdal Formation sandstones (2096.4-2107.4 m RKB). Final oil flow was 739 Sm3/day and final gas flow was 29.207 Sm3/day.

The AFE estimated time for the well was 28.1 days dry hole plus 10.5 days to DST. Actual estimated drilling time was 23.6 days, and testing was 9.8 days.

1.0 OBJECTIVES AND RISK

The discretionary exploration well 25/7-3 was drilled to test a 4 way dip closed structure (Elli South) approximately 3km south-south west of the Elli discovery well 25/8-5S.

The main objectives of the well were:

- To prove up commercial reserves for the 25/7-3 structure (Elli South) by testing the hydrocarbon potential of the Paleocene Upper Heimdal Formation.

- Define fluid contacts within the Heimdal Formation.

- Verify the structural mapping, depth conversion and geological model for the Elli South area.

- To provide sufficient data to start-up development planning.

- To provide a possible point of production should the results be positive.

- Obtain a good well tie to the top Cretaceous and top Balder seismic reflectors.

The well was drilled as planned to a total depth of 2540 m RKB, 55m into the Upper Cretaceous Tor Fm. and provide an important stratigraphic tie for further exploration along the western margin of the Utsira High.

The main risks were the top reservoir pick, oil water contact, geometry and lateral extent of the sandbodies, depth conversion and Net to Gross ratio within the Heimdal sands.

2.0 GEOLOGICAL SETTING

2.1 Tectonic Setting

Block 25/7 is situated in the South Viking Graben on the western side of the Utsira High, a basement high that tilts slightly towards the east. The South Viking Graben has an asymmetrical profile bounded in the west by the Brae/Crawford Fault Zone and the Utsira High to the east. The Elli Field is sitting on a basement terrace stepping up to the Utsira High from the Graben area.

The South Viking Graben was formed by major east-west extension during Late Permian to Early Triassic and Middle to Late Jurassic. The latter rifting phase with footwall uplift and subsequent erosion resulted in deposition of sands, clay and conglomerates along the western flank of the Utsira High and the eastern flank of the East Shetland Platform.

Two periods with significant tectonical uplift occurred in the North Sea. The first occurred in the Middle Jurassic and was centred around the Witch Graben, South Viking Graben and Central Graben triple junction. The second period of tectonic uplift started in the Latest Cretaceous and continued into the Paleocene and Early Eocene and was centred in the Irish Sea and the East Shetland platform area.

2.2 Structure and Trap

Well 25/7-3 tested a low relief 4 way dip closed structure at top Heimdal level (Elli South). The structure is located SSW of the Elli North structure which has been tested by the 25/8-5S and 25/8-6 wells. Most recent mapping of the area shows that the two structures are in communication as the mapped spill point between the two structures are shallower than the oil water contact in well 25/7-3. This is also confirmed by the common oil water contact (2091 mSS) observed in all the wells drilled in the area.

Run #1A

When running in hole, tool communication errors occurred at 50 metres. The tool string was pulled out of hole, and the cable was found to be shorted on all conductors. The problem was traced back to the pigtail connection between the wireline drum and collector ring on surface. The pigtail was changed out and logging was resumed and successfully completed.

Run #1B

In run #1B (ZDL/CN/MAC/SL), a computer panel in the logging unit failed, which caused downtime and later led to a MAC tool failure inside casing. Consequently, no MAC data was recorded above the 9-5/8" casing.

Run #1C

No operational problems occurred during the VSP log run. Last station was finished at 1200 m, the poor cement job behind 9-5/8" casing resulted in spotty VSP data.

5.0 GEOPHYSICAL RESULTS

A Zero offset VSP was acquired by READ Well Services on 13 - 14 August, 1995.

The seismic source employed was a 550 cu in Airgun with WSK. The source was positioned 3.5 m below MSL and operated at an air-pressure of 2000 psi. The receiver array consisted of a main tool and three satellites, each containing a 3-component geophone cartridge.

A total of 130 levels were recorded. The spacing was 10 m for the interval from 2520 m to 1680 and 20 m for the interval from 1680 m to 1160 m. Additional levels were shot with the main tool positioned at 2455 m, 2155 m, 2055m, and 1935 (all depths MD RKB).

The final data are of good to very good quality. Figure 4 shows composite display of the seismic surface and the corridor stack and shows a very good tie.

Well 25/7-2 largely confirmed the seismic interpretation as presented in the Drilling Program. Higher velocities than predicted were observed in the well which resulted in the main horizons coming in deeper than the prognosed depths. In addition Top Heimdal had been picked too high on the seismic. This combined with the increased velocities resulted in the Top Heimdal coming in 24 m deeper than prognosed.

Table 8 shows the prognosed vs. actual time/depth relation for the main horizons.

8.0 HYDROCARBON INDICATORS

8.1 Gas Shows

Routine analysis of ditch gas started from drilling out of the 13-3/8" casing shoe at 1179m MD. Gas data are listed in table 12.

In the Hordaland Group (991 - 1936.5 m MD) total gas readings varied from 0.1% to 1.0%. In the upper part of the section background gas levels were generally low, 0.1% to 0.3%, with slightly higher values in the Skade Formation, where the maximum was 0.5%. From 1600 m there was a gradual gas increase, and the first connection gas at 1680 m was 1.8%. From 1680 m to 1936.5 m the gas values were in the range of 0.3% to 1.0%. The chromatographic breakdown were mainly represented by C1 but with traces of C2 present from 1436 m, C3 present from 1472 m and C4 present from 1563 m.

(At 1680 m MD small amount of splintery shales were observed in the cuttings. The D-exponent showed a decreasing trend from 1325 m down to 1750 m. Maximum pore pressure gradient was reached at 1740 m where the well was close to balance. The mud weight was increased to 1.5 at this depth.)

In the Rogaland Group (1936.5 - 2484.5m MD) gas levels ranged from 0.1 to 0.6 %. In the top 8 1/2" hole section, from 1965 m to 2094 m, the background gas levels ranged from approximately 0.1 - 0.6 %. In the top Heimdal Formation a trip gas of 2.95 % was recorded when pulling out prior to cut the first core.

In the first coring interval (2099 m - 2110.8 m) the background gas levels were in the range from 0.1 % to 0.4 %, and 1.6 % trip gas was recorded from 2111 m. The chromatographic breakdown shows mainly C1 but good traces of C2, C3, C4 and even C5 (maximum 189 ppm C5 at 2105 m).

In the second coring interval (2111 m to 2130.15 m) the background gas levels were 0.2 - 0.6 % and 1.1 % trip gas was recorded at 2130 m. (The gas from 2112 m to 2124 m was not circulated to surface ??)

The interval drilled from 2130 m to 2484 m had background gas levels ranging from 0.1 - 0.6 %. The chromatographic breakdown was represented by C1, C2 and traces of C3 and occasionally C4.

In the Shetland Group (2484.5m - 2540m MD TD) gas levels were still low. Gas values were ranging from 0.1% to 0.6%, mostly C1 with traces of C2, C3 and rare C4 present. From a wiper trip prior to setting the 7" liner a trip gas of 1.7% was recorded at 2540 m TD.

11.0 PETROPHYSICAL REPORT

11.1 Log analysis (CPI 1:200 scale attached as enclosure)

All wireline logs were acquired and edited, including depth shifts, by Western Atlas. The logs used in the analysis were then borehole corrected as necessary. The Spectral Gamma was corrected for potassium content in the mud and hole size corrected, the Z Densilog was hole size corrected, the Dual Laterolog resistivity curves were corrected for borehole effects, and the Compensated Neutron curve was corrected for all borehole effects. The analysis of this well was done as a part of a multi-well study, which also included the 25/8-5S, 25/8-6, 25/8-6 T2, and the 25/8-8S, all of which are in the Elli / Tau discovery area. The analysis focused on the Heimdal sands, as they were the only ones containing hydrocarbons, however the analysis was done over the Sele - Ty interval. All corrections and analyses were done using Logstar, the in-house Conoco evaluation program.

The analysis for well 25/7-3 was not straightforward in that the upper part of the Heimdal Fm. contains shale clasts and lenses which depressed the resistivity response. Even the two primary sand units are too thin for the deep laterolog to resolve correctly. To account for this, a form of resistivity forward modeling was applied.

Petrophysical Model

The overall petrophysical model consists of a combination of several different models. Schlumberger Volan \( ^{1} \) type logic was applied in the computation of clay and silt volumes. Using information from the core analysis, a porosity was computed which provided the best fit to the core data. Fluid saturation and permeability were computed using the Archie equation, capillary pressure relationships, and sound geologic reasoning.

Clay and Shale Volume Computation

Clay volume was computed from a weighted average of a non-linear transform of the gamma ray, a linear transform of the gamma ray divided by bulk density, and density / neutron. The average is a Hodges-Lehmann weighted average, which is described in an 1982 SPWLA paper by Coates, et al \( ^{1} \) .

According to whole core descriptions of the Heimdal sands in the 25/7-3, they consist of a mix of high-density turbidites, muddy sandstones, low-density turbidites, carbonate-cemented sandy shale, injected/slumped sands, and shales. They range in grain size from medium to very fine, and in sorting from well to poorly sorted \( ^{2} \) . The top five meters is a heterolithic mix of each of these facies, and as such was fairly poorly resolved by the logging tools. The high sample rate density, neutron and spectral gamma tools, with their 0.3 meter resolution, described the clay volume the best. A detailed grain size description was used as a guide in

the clay and shale volume analysis. In this analysis, clay volume is comprised of dry clay and bound water.

Shale volume, which includes silt and other shale related material, was computed from hydrocarbon corrected density and neutron. Since some of the sands are very fine grained and / or poorly sorted, the computation of shale volume is important in defining permeability and highlighting sandy trends. The computation of shale volume is described in a 1970 JPT paper by Poupon, et al \( ^{3} \) .

Porosity Computation

Porosity was computed from the bulk density log using a technique which allows matrix density ( \( \rho ma \) ) to vary with varying porosity \( ^{4} \) . This technique uses measured core grain densities and porosities to compute a core "bulk density" ( \( \rho bc \) ) when an appropriate fluid density ( \( \rho f \) ) is assumed:

\[
\rho b c = (\phi c o r e * \rho f) + (1 - \phi c o r e) * \rho m a
\]

Core bulk density was crossplotted against core porosity, Figure 6, and the resulting linear regression was used to compute log porosity from the bulk density log. Where clay volume was greater than 35%, which defines net sand, porosity was multiplied by (1 - Vclay), to give an effective porosity in the shales and aid in the computation of permeability.

Fluid Saturation Computation

Since the Dual Laterolog resistivities in the uppermost Heimdal Fm. are adversely affected by shale clasts and the overall thin bedded nature of the sands in the 25/7-3, a form of resistivity forward modeling was utilized for the prediction of deep resistivity for use in the computation of fluid saturation. Above the transition zone fluid saturation was computed from a linear regression of pore throat radius and Archie derived water saturation, Figure 7, because on the petrophysical relationship between fluid saturation, pore geometry (size, shape and sorting of the pore throats) of the sands and structural position in the hydrocarbon column \( ^{5} \) . Pore throat radius was computed using the transform described by Kolodzie \( ^{6} \) , and Pittman \( ^{7} \) , which is:

\[
L o g R 3 5 = 0. 7 3 2 + 0. 5 8 8 L o g K - 0. 8 6 4 L o g \phi
\]

where R35 = pore throat radius at 35% pore volume, in microns

In the transition zone and in the water sands, fluid saturation was computed using the Archie equation and the deep laterolog. Figure 8 shows the comparison between Sw computed using the deep laterolog and the Archie equation, and the enhanced Sw. It also shows the deep laterolog versus the forward modeled Rt.

Permeability Computation

The permeability computation utilized input from the porosity, clay volume and silt index. The transform is stated:

\[
\begin{array}{l} L o g K = 1 2 * \phi - 6 * S I ^ {1. 5} - 8 * V c l y ^ {3} \\ S I = \text { silt   index,   which   is } V s h l - V c l y \\ \end{array}
\]

where \(\phi = \log\) derived porosity (fraction) as described above

\(V_{c}ly =\) clay volume (fraction) as described above

\(Vshl =\) shale volume (fraction) as described above

\(K =\) permeability in millidarcies

Porosity is the dominant input into this transform, but it also takes into account grain size and the degree of sorting by incorporating the Vcly / Vshl terms. This allows for a more accurate permeability estimation as facies change. Results compare favorably with whole core klinkenberg corrected horizontal permeability, Figure 8; and the geometric average of the log derived permeability compares very well with DST data.

Discussion of Results

New methodology has dramatically improved the petrophysical characterization of the sands encountered in well 25/7-3. Results match core and drill stem test data. The average hydrocarbon saturation for the net Heimdal sands has been increased by approximately 11%, or 0.72 versus 0.64, as compared to computing Sw using a conventional approach.

1.4 Equipment Inspections

A. CNI accepted risk by not inspecting the drill string to DEQS standards. There were no problems with tubular connections during the 25/7-3 operations and the inspection arrangement allowed the rig to be moved to location with drill pipe in the derrick, thereby saving the cost and time to pick up and lay down tubulars at location.

• Drill collars and subs were inspected to API standards.

- 30 joints of 5" S135 drill pipe were inspected in accordance with API premium class specs. This was done as a spot check to verify the condition of the string and was deemed acceptable since the pipe was new in October 1994 and had not been subjected to harsh conditions.

B. A third party inspector was contracted to inspect the BOP stack and related equipment. This was beneficial since several potentially problematic items were identified. The well control equipment performed flawlessly during the well operations.

1.5 Information Management

A. Rig communications were routed through Statoil's Forus office with no apparent problems. Statoil equipment and systems were utilized as much as possible to reduce costs and lead time.

1.6 Application for Consent to Drill

The rig was handed over to CNI much quicker than originally planned. Consequently, the ACD process was much quicker than normal. Some of the items that allowed the ACD to be completed in such a short time follow.

A. Many ACD documents that were prepared by Statoil were used for the 25/7-3.

B. An oil spill contingency plan developed by Amerada Hess, another partner in PL103, was used.

C. Bringing in an ODCC engineer and Conoco rig supervisor to help prepare documentation greatly helped the process.

D. A blowout scenario that was prepared for the relief well plan for the Heidrun pre-drilling project was used for the 25/7-3 case, as the assumed blowout scenario was considered similar, but worse, than would be expected at Elli.

E. ODCC had a high-quality safety case that had already highlighted operational hazards and areas of concern.

ResultsPlanned time: 29.7 hoursActual time: 16.5 hoursThe Deepsea Bergen was on contract to Conoco at 1305 hrs on 26/7/95 when the rig was under tight tow in the Haugesund harbor. The M/V "Aldoma", a 12 kHP AHTS, was used to tow the DSB from Haugesund to the 25/7-3 location at an overall average of 6.6 knots. The 8½" hole was drilled to total depth at 2540m, 52m past the top Cretaceous. Caliper logs showed the hole to be in gauge.

C. Observations and Lessons Learned

1. An 8½" IADC 1-3-5 was used to drill to core point. Average ROP was slightly lower than the end of the 12¼" section, which may have been a function of the motor and PDC bit that was used in the previous section. The bit was graded 2-2. The 8½" section appears to have PDC bit application to the base Heimdal, although caution is given to the several hard streaks in the Heimdal.

2. MW was cut back and maintained to 1.2 sg for the entire hole section. Glycol was maintained at 3% and KCl was 110 kg/m3 at the shaker. The hole was calipered in gauge to near-gauge, but it was necessary to backream to the shoe and 8m of hard fill were washed and reamed on the wiper trip. Logs encountered 7m of fill. The fill appeared to have been sloughs from the Balder and Lista formations.

3. The 8½" section below the Heimdal is much firmer and had a much lower ROP. Combinations of gummy clays and hard, cemented sandstones and limestone stringers made drilling slow. The Cretaceous is extremely hard - the 52m of Cretaceous were drilled at 3 m/hr.

4. The section below the Heimdal was drilled with one ATMGT18 insert bit. The bit was graded 8-8-LT-N-4-RG-TD. Two of the seals and bearings were not effective, the cones had no compacts left, two cones were cracked and the bit was undergauge. The Heimdal sands were easily drilled at 40-60 m/hr.

5. The section was drilled much faster than prognosed since the section was drilled in only one bit run and the overall ROP was faster than prognosed.

### OBJECTIVE:

At TD of the 17 1/2" hole section the inclination was 3 deg inclination in 133 deg azimuth.
The objective for the run was to make a correction run to drop the inclination back to vertical
and continue to drill 12 1/4" hole vertical to TD of the section. Last survey station 17 1/2"
section was at 1178m which showed 3.0 deg inclination in 130.2 deg azimuth.


BHA # 2          1179m-1965 m                          9 1/2" NAVIDRILL AKO ASSY

A 9 1/2" Navidrill MK1 P/HF AKO with s/n 1516 was picked up and made up to a 12 1/4"
Hycadog PDC bit dressed with 4x14 and 4x15 jets. The AKO was set to 0.9 deg which equals
a DLS of 4.0/30m. Aligned the motor scribeline and tested both motor and MWD to
specifications prior to RIH.

Drilled out the cement/float/shoetrack and 3m of new formation down to 1189m prior to
perform a LOT. Continued to drill in rotary mode to 1211m where the MWD was free of
magnetic interference. Oriented in a 300-320 deg. magnetic toolface drilling to drop the
inclination back to vertical in intervals as needed. The motor gave good response and the
well was vertical at +/-1308m. After the last orientation the survey station at 1337m showed
0.8deg in 315.8 deg azimuth. This was as planned and the well now corrected in the opposite
direction towards the target. The remaining part of the 12 1/4" hole section was drilled in
rotary mode. The BHA showed a slightly build tendency in rotary mode of 0.06deg/30m and
basically held direction. Drilled to 9 5/8" casing point at 1965m and last survey station at
1948m showed 2.1 deg inclination in 315.2 deg azimuth. The well was back to the original
plan and the objective of the run was met. POOH without any problems.

The 12 1/4" section was drilled fast and very efficient with the 9 1/2" Navidrill MK1 P/HF.
The run have proven that a motor assembly gives 100 % directional control in a vertical
well and only minor corrections are needed to keep the well on track.. This run has also
proven the motor has an advantage to optimise the drilling and are strongly recommended
in the future to be used for performance drilling .

## Summary Of Drilling Events:

This section was drilled in just over 18 hours using a Hycalog DS 70 HF bit with a TFA of 1.29 in2. A steerable mud motor assembly was used to control the inclination to as near vertical as possible. After drilling 3 metres of new formation with seawater, an FIT was made to 1.57 SG EMW (with seawater and a 100 m column of prehydrated gel mud at the bottom of the hole). The hole was then displaced with 1.46 SG Anco 2000. An average ROP of 43 metres per hour was achieved through the predominantly claystone/shale interval. As a consequence of small concentrations of splintered shale and 2% connection gas at 1965 m, the mud weight was increased to 1.50 SG.

No problems were encountered in drilling to 1965 metres. Slight overpull (maximum = 15 T) was observed on the trip prior to running casing. It was necessary to wash to bottom while running the final joints of 9 5/8" casing; 25 metres of fill was reported. The casing was set @ 1958 m.

During the cementing operation, a total of 132 m3 were lost to the formation. The Skade formation (porous sandstone), just below the 13 3/8" shoe, was speculated to be the most likely interval for the losses to occur. Indications were that the cement job was successful. The cement was displaced with 1.20 SG mud prior to pulling out of the hole.

Shale Shakers

60R/100R mesh screens were used initially to minimize losses as a consequence of the low temperature and the viscous new mud. Solids control performance:

Screen combinations of 80R/120R or 150R and 100R over 150R controlled the shale cuttings/limestone and sands well, with some additional running of the centrifuge and mud cleaner for occasional weight control and to hasten the reduction in sand content. The mud cleaner continues to have limited effectiveness (see previous section Solids Control Performance discussion).

The Gann shale shakers do not - despite regular maintenance - appear to be working at all well. The mud "dances" vertically on the screens and pools of solids/degrading cuttings collect towards the rear. Attempts have been made to vary the speed of vibration but it appears that the vibration is either not enough or the motion of the shakers is not adequate for the purpose. This was not a particularly heavy or thick mud and serious thought needs to be given to aspects of the solids control equipment on this rig as with the cost of fluids these days it is a false economy to run less than excellent shakers and mud cleaners, even though a limited perspective may suggest it to be less costly. Now that water based fluids are being "re-cycled" from well to well solids (particularly fines) are the main limitation in many cases.

1.0 Objectives

MWD and electric line logs indicated the presence of a hydrocarbon bearing interval in the uppermost Heimdal of well 25/7-3 from 2094.4-2114.5 mRKB. FMT logs indicated the hydrocarbons were oil but that there was an oil-water-contact at 2114.5 mRKB. In order to evaluate the potential of the oil bearing section of the Heimdal reservoir a single drill stem test program was conducted from 15-24 August 1995 across the interval from 2096.4-2107.4 mRKB (reference ZDL/CNL/GR of 13 August 1995). The primary technical objectives of the well testing program were as follows:

1. To determine the movable fluids in the reservoir.

2. To obtain representative samples of the movable fluids.

3. To evaluate the flowing potential and productivity of the well.

4. To evaluate the near well bore description through pressure transient analysis.

5. To obtain information on the reservoir region away from the well bore through analysis of the late time pressure transient data.

The operational objectives of the test program were:

1. Conduct all well testing operations without a single lost-time accident.

2. Complete all well testing operations within the time and budgetary limits established in the AFE.

3. Successfully handle and dispose all hydrocarbons while minimizing any effect on the environment.

2.0 Test Results Summary

The well flowed low GOR oil at a reasonably high rate considering the short perforation interval. This is encouraging as analysis of the pressure transient data indicated that the reservoir pressure was less than normal. The 25/8-5S well also had a less than normal reservoir pressure gradient.

Analysis of the main buildup pressure transient data revealed the presence of spherical flow throughout the majority of the buildup. This could be due to increased thickening of the perforated interval away from the wellbore or due to communication with the mid/lower Heimdal reservoir sands which begin at approximately 2111 mRKB. This would indicate that the shales between the upper Heimdal and mid/lower Heimdal sections may not be fully sealing since interpretation of the geologic data indicates the shales are laterally continuous.

Vetco originally provided dimensions for the shorter wearbushing but ultimately, the longer wearbushing was run and set in the wellhead. POST WELL - SITE SURVEY REPORT/SHALLOW GAS REPORT

Shallow geology and shallow gas

No shallow gas was prognosed for this well location, and no evidence of gas was seen during the drilling operation.

The Site Survey for the well was carried out as a part of a larger Regional Site Survey by Britsurvey, a division of Svitzer Limited. This was acquired using the vessel M.V. "Svitzer Magellan" during the period, 24th April to 21st May 1995.

The regional survey covered an area of approximately 18 x 14 kilometres and consisted of 856.9 line kilometres (71 lines with 500 metre spacing) of integrated analogue (sidescan sonar, multibeam echosounder, Bentech subbottom profiler, single channel airgun) and digital multichannel seismic data.

The ES-94-3 3D seismic dataset was also used for the shallow geological interpretation.

Top Skade formation was considered when determining the casing point for the surface casing string, as it was expected to be a weaker sandy formation and was to be avoided with the casing shoe. Predicted depth from the Site Survey data was within < 2 metres of that observed in the well.

A 36" hole was drilled to 227 metres RKB and 30" casing set at 223 metres RKB. A 17-1/2" hole was then drilled to 1186 metres RKB and 13-3/8" casing set at 1179 metres RKB. No pilot hole was drilled on this well due to the lack of shallow gas indicators from the Site Survey and absence of any indications of gas in the nearby 25/8-5S and 25/8-6 wells.
